entries.clue: When the world’s not ready for enemies to be trounced (6,4,4)

indicatorNotes.trounced: the letters are beaten into a new shape

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: A general waits until his foes are ready to be defeated, a battle-plan picture.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To be' looks like part of the grammar of the sentence, but it is fodder: all fourteen letters from 'for' to 'be' are used.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone ahead of their time lives before the world is ready for their ideas.

entries.clue: Bay that’s included principally in Shipping Forecasts – in the middle? (6)

indicatorNotes.included: the letters I, S, C are put inside BAY
indicatorNotes.principally: take the first letters of 'included' and 'Shipping'

blocks.note: the outer word, split B…AY
first letters of 'included' and 'Shipping'
C is the fifth of FORECASTS' nine letters

annotation.surface: A radio listener hears the Shipping Forecast read out, with one sea area somewhere in the middle of it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bay' does double duty as definition and the container. Biscay is also one of the sea areas named in the BBC's Shipping Forecast, a radio bulletin for sailors around Britain, so the whole clue describes the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: The Bay of Biscay lies off western France and northern Spain.

entries.clue: Loudly punished faceless aficionado, suppressing resistance and getting bird (9,6)

indicatorNotes.suppressing: FIEND holds R down inside it

blocks.note: f = forte, loudly in music
LEATHERED (beaten) without its first letter
a fiend = an enthusiast, as in 'fitness fiend'
R = resistance in physics, placed inside FIEND

annotation.surface: A fan who has been noisily punished and disfigured, while holding back resistance, somehow ends up with a bird.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Faceless' looks like it goes with 'aficionado', but it acts on 'punished': LEATHERED is British slang for beaten. 'Loudly' is a single letter, not a sound clue.
annotation.definitionFit: An affectionate, slightly jokey idiom for any bird, especially a pet one.

entries.clue: Survives; leaves on horseback (5,3)

blocks.note: as a ship gets through a storm without sinking
literal: sets off from the stable mounted

annotation.surface: A cavalry officer escapes danger by galloping away.
annotation.walkthrough: The semicolon splits the two meanings cleanly; the second is literal, the first is the idiom of weathering a crisis.
annotation.definitionFit: To ride out a crisis is to survive it without being overwhelmed.

entries.clue: Monster, therefore recoiling! (4)

blocks.note: ergo = therefore, from Latin
reversal indicator

annotation.surface: Someone shrinks back in horror at a monster.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Recoiling' fits the surface as a fright at the monster, which hides its job of turning ERGO round.
annotation.definitionFit: An ogre is a man-eating giant of folk tales.

entries.clue: Hid rabid deerhounds (10)

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Someone hides from a pack of mad hunting dogs.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hid' reads as a verb about someone fleeing the dogs; ENSHROUDED is the past tense of covering something up.
annotation.definitionFit: To enshroud is to wrap or conceal, so enshrouded means hid.

entries.clue: Some extra umami gives you shock (6)

indicatorNotes.Some: only part of the following words is taken

blocks.note: the last three letters of 'extra' run on into the first three of 'umami'

annotation.surface: An unexpectedly strong savoury flavour startles a diner.
annotation.walkthrough: The food vocabulary makes 'shock' read as a jolt to the taste buds; umami is the savoury fifth taste.
annotation.definitionFit: Trauma is a severe shock, physical or emotional.

entries.clue: Makes destiny etc go awry, and bites the dust (5,1,6,3)

indicatorNotes.go awry: the letters go wrong and end up out of order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Someone who sends fate off course comes to a bad end.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Makes' looks like the verb of the sentence, but it is part of the fodder; without it the letters fall far short.
annotation.definitionFit: To bite the dust and to meet a sticky end both mean to die, usually unpleasantly.

entries.clue: Old songs and flags (9)

blocks.note: long-established songs every singer covers, like 'My Funny Valentine'
a standard is a flag, as in the royal standard

annotation.surface: A parade features old tunes and waving banners.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flags' could be a verb (tires); here it is a plural noun.
annotation.definitionFit: Standards are well-established songs that performers keep returning to.

entries.clue: Élite group had some food before noon (1-4)

blocks.note: ate = had food
a.m. = before noon

annotation.surface: The top squad took an early lunch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Before noon' reads as when the meal happened, but it is the abbreviation AM.
annotation.definitionFit: An A-team is the best group of people available for a job.

entries.clue: Leisurely walks? Brief moments – engrossing, on reflection, I’d be glad to! (6)

indicatorNotes.engrossing: MOS takes the other word into itself
indicatorNotes.on reflection: a reflection shows the word backwards

blocks.note: mo = a moment, short for 'half a mo'
an eager yes, turned round to SEY

annotation.surface: Someone invited for a stroll replies after a moment's thought that they would love to.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I'd be glad to' sounds like dialogue, but it is a definition of YES. The question mark flags that MOSEYS is a verb used loosely as a plural noun.
annotation.definitionFit: To mosey is to amble in a leisurely way; moseys are leisurely walks.

entries.clue: Woods may hold such sporting prize (5)

blocks.note: ash trees grow in woods
the small urn England and Australia play Test cricket for

annotation.surface: A golfer called Woods might be holding a trophy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Woods' at the start of the clue is capitalised anyway, so it passes as Tiger Woods holding a prize; it is really a forest.
annotation.definitionFit: Ashes are trees; the Ashes is the Test cricket series and urn contested by England and Australia.

entries.clue: Property of theses (8)

blocks.note: a building and its grounds, as in 'no smoking on the ...'
propositions an argument starts from

annotation.surface: An academic's arguments are treated as if they were real estate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Property of' reads as 'characteristic of'; it is a noun, buildings and land.
annotation.definitionFit: Premises are both a building with its land and the propositions an argument starts from.

entries.clue: It comes out at night offering support to a hunter (6,4)

annotation.definition: It comes out at night offering support to a hunter

blocks.note: the surface suggests an owl or a bat; it is a group of stars appearing after dark
the Hunter is a constellation, and what supports his trousers is a belt

annotation.surface: A nocturnal creature helps a huntsman.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads like an owl or a bat assisting someone on a hunt; the thing that comes out at night is a row of stars.
annotation.definitionFit: Orion's Belt is the line of three stars across the middle of the Hunter constellation.

entries.clue: 44 runs to the west twice: fancy! (4-4)

indicatorNotes.runs to the west: the R (runs) moves leftwards in each FOUR

blocks.note: 4 and 4 read as the words FOUR FOUR
R, the cricket abbreviation for runs, shifts left in each FOUR

annotation.surface: A cricket scorecard shows 44 runs made on the western side, twice, and someone is impressed.
annotation.walkthrough: '44' is two digits, each spelt out as FOUR; moving R forward in each turns FOUR into FROU. 'Twice' confirms the doubling.
annotation.definitionFit: Frou-frou means fussy, frilly ornamentation, so it works as an adjective for fancy.

entries.clue: Glimpse, with psychic powers, yeti’s head (4)

indicatorNotes.head: the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: ESP = extrasensory perception
first letter of 'yeti'

annotation.surface: A clairvoyant catches sight of the abominable snowman's head.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a psychic sighting a yeti, which is roughly what the answer does.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, if a literary one: both mean catching sight of something briefly or from afar.

entries.clue: Detective’s addresses in the auditorium (6)

indicatorNotes.in the auditorium: an auditorium is where things are heard

blocks.note: addresses = homes, the places people live; the spelling adds a silent L

annotation.surface: A detective gives speeches to a theatre audience.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Addresses' reads as speeches, but it means homes. The apostrophe-s is 'is', linking definition to wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Sherlock Holmes is the most famous fictional detective.

entries.clue: Protégée given to aunts announced preparation for hostilities (3,5)

indicatorNotes.announced: said out loud, so it is the sound that counts

annotation.surface: A young charge is handed over to her aunts, and war is declared.
annotation.walkthrough: The homophone only works where 'aunts' is said with a short a; in southern British speech it sounds like 'ahnts'.
annotation.definitionFit: A war dance is performed to rouse fighters before battle.

entries.clue: Twee ‘antique’, golden, uncased (4)

blocks.note: GOLDEN without its first and last letters

annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks around 'antique' signal the mock-old spelling, as in 'Ye Olde Tea Shoppe'.
annotation.definitionFit: Olde is a twee, fake-antique spelling of old.

entries.clue: Primarily orotund, pronouncedly emotively rococo; alternatively, that involves Carmen? (8)

entries.clue: Spot sharp implement taking some measure (6)

annotation.walkthrough: 'Measure' reads as a ruler's job for the implement; with 'taking some' it means a portion of the letters.

entries.clue: Historical periods ultimately come together (I’ll correct writer’s mistakes) (6)

last letters of 'come' and 'together'

entries.clue: Most like Friar Tuck, squiffier than the rest (8)

annotation.definitionFit: Friar Tuck is the jolliest of Robin Hood's Merry Men, and merriest is also most tipsy.

entries.clue: Democrat you may know as Republican: capital! (5)

annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital!' reads as an old-fashioned cry of approval; it is the definition, a capital city.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the city is Senegal's capital, on the West African coast.

entries.clue: Doors increasingly left open in winter? (6,8)
